newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: South Africa breaks impasse in EU trade talks.
newsitem.headline: South Africa breaks impasse in EU trade talks.

text.p: South Africa broke an impasse on Friday in stalled trade talks with the European Union by outlining its position and presenting a long-awaited negotiating mandate to EU officials.
Department of Trade and Industry director of trade relations Bahle Sibisi said the mandate was handed over during a meeting in Pretoria.
"We met this morning with the EU representative here and handed over a document on South Africa's basis for negotiations on a trade and development agreement," he said by telephone from Pretoria.
The move paves the way for the resumption of formal negotiations between the two sides in South Africa at the end of next month, he said.

Sibisi declined to detail South Africa's position but said the negotiating document was the culmination of extensive consultation with South African business, labour, parliamentary and public interests.
Brussels set out its own negotiating position back in March, but its mandate was slammed by a number of influential parties in South Africa as being too harsh on South Africa and its neighbours.
The EU has refused post-apartheid South Africa full accession to the Lome Convention which grants favourable access to its markets to developing countries in Africa, the Caribbean and the Pacific.

Instead Brussels produced a mandate which would exclude nearly 40 percent of South Africa's agricultural products from a future free trade deal, while calling on it to reduce tariffs to ensure easier access to its markets for European producers.

That caused ructions within South Africa, including fierce criticism from parliamentarians who claimed the EU had failed to take into account the very different sizes and levels of development of the economies of the negotiating partners.
The EU for its part criticised South Africa for dragging its heels in presenting its own position.

There have also been growing concerns within the southern Africa region about the impact of a free trade deal between Pretoria and Brussels on the economies of some of South Africa's smaller neighbours.
Other members of the five-nation South Africa Customs Union (SACU) -- Botswana, Namibia, Lesotho and Swaziland -- fear they will lose millions in income from the joint customs revenue pool.
Sibisi said South Africa's mandate took account of these concerns within SACU, as well as views from the wider 12-nation Southern African Development Community.
Some 40 percent of South Africa's exports go to EU member states and more than one third of its imports are of EU origin.
